fonte.referencia: Texto fictício escrito para estudo, no formato de artigo de revisão

texto.nota: Texto fictício, escrito para estudo no formato de um artigo de revisão. Autores, periódico, citações, estudos e dados numéricos são inventados; os conceitos biológicos descritos (enxameação, batedoras, dança do requebrado, sinal de parada, quórum) são gerais.
texto.titulo: Thinking without a brain? Nest-site selection in honeybee swarms and the limits of ‘distributed intelligence’
texto.abstract: This article reviews research on how swarms of the western honeybee choose a new nest site and asks what, if anything, the process reveals about ‘distributed intelligence’. The biological problem is first outlined: a swarm of several thousand bees, having left its parent colony, must select a single cavity among dispersed alternatives within a few days, although no individual bee compares them. Competing definitions of ‘collective intelligence’ and ‘swarm intelligence’ are then compared, and it is argued that the looser uses of these terms obscure more than they explain. Four mechanisms are subsequently examined: the independent assessment of cavities by scouts, recruitment through the waggle dance, cross-inhibition through stop signals, and quorum sensing at the candidate site. The trade-off between speed and accuracy is discussed, as are analogies with neural decision-making, human groups and robot swarms. It is concluded that the swarm is best described not as an intelligent agent but as a decision mechanism whose reliability depends on specific and fragile conditions, which are rarely all met in the systems to which it is compared.
texto.keywords: honeybee, swarm intelligence, collective decision-making, nest-site selection, waggle dance, quorum sensing

blocos.p: In late spring and early summer, a honeybee colony that has outgrown its cavity reproduces by division. The old queen departs with roughly two thirds of the workers – typically between 8,000 and 15,000 bees in temperate populations – while a daughter queen, reared in the preceding weeks, inherits the parent nest together with the remaining workers, the brood and the stored honey. Within minutes of leaving, the departing bees settle as a dense cluster on a branch or a similar support, usually a few metres from the original nest, and it is from this temporary bivouac that the search for a permanent home is conducted. The cluster has no comb, no brood and no stores apart from the honey that its members carried in their stomachs when they left. It is, in effect, a homeless colony, and the decision it now faces is among the most consequential it will ever make.

The difficulty of that decision lies in two requirements that pull in opposite directions. On the one hand, the swarm must decide quickly: the honey carried by its workers has been estimated to sustain the cluster for no more than three or four days (Halvorsen-Teague, 2009), and an exposed cluster is vulnerable to rain, cold and predators. On the other hand, it must decide well, since the cavity selected will have to shelter the colony through the following winter, and a cavity that is too small to hold sufficient honey, too damp or too exposed is likely to prove fatal months after the choice has been made. This double bind is what makes nest-site selection an unusually clean test case for the study of collective decisions. Because the outcome can be measured, the time taken can be recorded and the information available to each bee can be estimated, the process lends itself to experimental manipulation in a way that few decisions made by human groups do.

The interest of the case, however, extends well beyond apiculture. Over the past two decades, the honeybee swarm has been invoked as a model of democratic deliberation, as an inspiration for algorithms that coordinate fleets of drones and as an analogue of the way in which populations of neurons settle on a perceptual judgement (Okafor-Lindqvist, 2014; Brandvold, 2019). Such breadth of appeal is both an asset and a liability. It is an asset because a mechanism refined by natural selection over millions of years may suggest solutions which engineers and institutional designers would not otherwise have considered; it is a liability because the more widely a model is borrowed, the more likely it is that the conditions under which it works will be forgotten in transit. The present review is intended to recover those conditions. Section 2 compares the definitions under which the swarm has been described as intelligent; Sections 3 to 6 examine the mechanisms of the decision; Section 7 considers what can, and what cannot, be carried beyond the hive.

The term ‘collective intelligence’ has been defined in ways that differ less in wording than in what they require of a group. In the broadest formulation, Pellegrini-Achebe (2008, p. 12) describes it as ‘the capacity of a group to solve problems that none of its members could solve alone’. The definition has the merit of simplicity, but it sets no condition on how the problem is solved: a group in which one well-informed member dictates the answer to the others would satisfy it, provided that member could not have implemented the solution unaided. Rasmussen-Okoye (2012) narrows the field by requiring that the performance of the group exceed that of its best member, a criterion which excludes cases of mere delegation but which, in practice, has rarely been tested, because the performance of the best individual is seldom known.

Definitions of ‘swarm intelligence’, the narrower term most often applied to social insects, tend to emphasise mechanism rather than performance. For Dufresne-Kamau (2011), a system displays swarm intelligence when coherent group-level behaviour arises from local interactions among individuals that follow simple rules and have no access to global information. Tobiassen (2015, p. 87) adds a further requirement, namely that ‘no individual holds, or needs to hold, a representation of the problem as a whole’. The latter criterion fits the honeybee swarm closely: no scout visits more than a few of the candidate sites, and none is known to compare them. It is, however, a negative criterion, which specifies what individuals lack rather than what the group achieves, and it would be satisfied equally well by a swarm that consistently chose poor sites.

A third group of definitions locates intelligence in the relationship between a system and its environment. Ishikawa-Moreau (2017) proposes that a collective be called intelligent only to the extent that it adjusts its decision procedure to the demands of the situation, for example by trading accuracy for speed when time is short. On this view, the question is not whether a swarm reaches good decisions, nor whether it does so without a leader, but whether its procedure is itself responsive to conditions. Ishikawa-Moreau acknowledges that this is the most demanding of the definitions considered here and also the one for which the evidence from honeybees is thinnest (2017, p. 203). If the criterion is taken seriously, the experiments on quorum size reviewed in Section 6 acquire a significance beyond the biology of bees, since they are among the very few that bear on it directly.

Alongside these definitions, a looser usage has spread through both the scientific and the popular literature, in which ‘swarm intelligence’ is applied to almost any coordinated behaviour of many agents, such as the trail networks of ants, the synchronised flashing of fireflies and the price movements of financial markets. The cost of this extension is not merely terminological. When the same label is attached to phenomena that share no mechanism, findings obtained in one system are readily assumed to hold in another, and the conditions that made a group reliable in the original case drop out of view. Vasquez-Lindholm (2020) found that, in a sample of 164 articles which applied the term to engineered systems, fewer than one in four specified which features of the biological model were being borrowed. Throughout this review, the term is accordingly used in the restricted sense given by Dufresne-Kamau and Tobiassen, and claims about performance are kept separate from claims about mechanism.

blocos.h2: 3. Scouting and the assessment of cavities

blocos.p: The search begins before the swarm has left the parent nest. In the days preceding departure, a few dozen of the colony’s older foragers begin to inspect potential cavities, and once the cluster has formed, their number rises to between 300 and 500, which amounts to roughly three to five per cent of the swarm (Halvorsen-Teague, 2009). The remaining bees take no part in the search: they hang quietly in the cluster, conserving energy, until the moment of departure. Scouts fly out in all directions, and in a typical decision between 10 and 30 potential sites are discovered and reported, some of them several kilometres from the cluster.

Each scout that discovers a cavity inspects it thoroughly, in a visit that may last from 10 to 40 minutes and during which she walks repeatedly across its interior surfaces and flies in and out of its entrance. Several properties of the cavity appear to be assessed in this way. In a survey of 72 natural nests, Nwachukwu-Sorensen (2013) found that most occupied cavities had a volume of between 30 and 60 litres and an entrance smaller than 30 cm² located near the floor of the cavity and at least three metres above the ground; in temperate populations of the northern hemisphere, entrances facing south were also overrepresented. Those preferences are not arbitrary. A cavity of about 40 litres can hold enough comb and honey for a colony to survive the winter, a small entrance is easier to defend and to keep warm, and a high entrance is thought to reduce the risk of attack by ground-dwelling predators. How scouts measure these properties is less well understood. Volume, for instance, is thought to be estimated from the distance walked inside the cavity, which would explain why scouts spend much of their first visit on foot rather than on the wing.

Two features of the assessment deserve emphasis, because both turn out to be essential to the accuracy of the outcome. First, assessments are made independently. A scout evaluates only the site she has found or to which she has been recruited, and she does so on the basis of her own inspection rather than of the enthusiasm of the bees that recruited her. Second, no scout compares sites. In marking experiments, Feldmann-Ortiz (2016) observed that fewer than 5% of scouts visited more than one candidate site during a decision, and those that did were no more likely than the others to support the better of the two. The comparison of alternatives, in other words, is not performed by any bee; if it is performed at all, it is performed by the dynamics of the population of scouts, to which we now turn.

A scout that has inspected a promising cavity returns to the cluster and advertises it by means of the waggle dance, the same signal that foragers use to indicate sources of nectar and pollen. The dance is performed on the surface of the cluster and consists of a straight ‘waggle run’, during which the dancer vibrates her abdomen from side to side, followed by a return loop to the starting point, made alternately to the right and to the left. Two pieces of information are encoded in the waggle run. Its angle relative to the vertical corresponds to the direction of the site relative to the sun’s azimuth: a run straight upwards indicates a site in the direction of the sun, and a run 40° to the left of vertical a site 40° to the left of it. Its duration, by contrast, encodes distance, at a rate of roughly one second of waggling for each kilometre, although the exact calibration has been shown to vary between populations and with the terrain over which the bee has flown (Rourke-Almeida, 2018).

What the dance does not encode directly is quality. Quality is conveyed instead by how much a scout dances: scouts returning from superior cavities perform more waggle runs, and dance more vigorously, than scouts returning from mediocre ones, and scouts returning from poor cavities often do not dance at all. In observations of 14 swarms, Rourke-Almeida (2018) recorded a mean of 92 waggle runs after a first visit to a high-quality site, compared with 31 after a first visit to a low-quality one. Because unemployed scouts in the cluster follow dancers more or less at random, a site that is advertised more strongly is visited by more recruits, who in turn return to dance for it if their own inspection is favourable. The result is a positive feedback in which the number of bees committed to each site grows at a rate that reflects its quality.

Positive feedback alone, however, would be a recipe for error, since a site that happened to be discovered early could accumulate supporters regardless of its merits. The danger is reduced by a feature that has proved central to every subsequent model of the process: the gradual decline in the number of waggle runs performed by each returning scout. On each successive return, a scout dances somewhat less than on the previous one – by roughly 15 runs per trip, according to Rourke-Almeida (2018) – until, after a few hours, she stops dancing altogether, whatever the quality of her site. Support for any site must therefore be continually renewed by fresh recruits, each of whom has inspected the site independently. A site whose early lead rests on chance rather than quality loses that lead as its original supporters fall silent, whereas a superior site continues to attract new dancers. The decline thus functions as a kind of forgetting, which prevents the swarm from becoming locked into its first impressions.

A second negative feedback operates between rather than within groups of supporters. A scout that has committed to one site will frequently approach a bee dancing for a different site and deliver a ‘stop signal’: a brief vibration, lasting about a tenth of a second, produced while she butts her head against the dancer. Dancers that receive repeated stop signals tend to cut their dances short. In a study in which two nest boxes of equal quality were offered, Andrade-Kowalczyk (2019) found that more than 60% of the stop signals received by dancers for one box were delivered by scouts that had visited the other, a pattern which indicates that the signal is directed preferentially at rivals rather than at fellow supporters. Comparable signals are used by foragers to inhibit recruitment to food sources at which they have been attacked, and it is from this foraging signal that the one used during nest-site selection has probably been derived. In the vocabulary of debate that has grown up around the swarm, the stop signal is the closest thing the hive has to heckling a rival speaker: it does not argue for one site so much as silence the advocates of another.

The effect of cross-inhibition is most evident when sites are of similar quality. Without it, two equally good sites would tend to accumulate supporters in parallel, and the swarm could remain divided indefinitely or, worse, split, with part of the swarm flying to each site. Such deadlocks are rare in nature, and simulations by Andrade-Kowalczyk and Lindqvist-Obi (2021) suggest why: when the rate of stop signalling exceeds a modest threshold, small random differences between the two groups of supporters are amplified, so that one group suppresses the other and a choice is made even between options whose merits are indistinguishable. The price of doing so is that the choice between equal sites becomes, in effect, arbitrary, which matters little when the alternatives are equivalent but would matter considerably if the signal were directed at superior sites as often as at inferior ones.

blocos.h2: 6. Quorum sensing, take-off and the speed–accuracy trade-off

blocos.p: How, then, does the swarm know that a decision has been reached? The answer, which long ran contrary to intuition, is that it does not need to know. No consensus is ever registered at the cluster, and the dancers often still disagree at the moment of departure. The ‘debate’ in the cluster, in other words, is never formally closed; it is simply overtaken by events elsewhere. Instead, the decision is triggered at the sites themselves. Scouts visiting a cavity appear to monitor the number of other scouts present there, and once that number reaches a threshold – estimated at between 20 and 30 bees by Feldmann-Ortiz (2016) – they change their behaviour. Rather than dancing, they return to the cluster and begin to produce ‘piping’ signals, a high-pitched vibration which stimulates the quiescent bees to warm their flight muscles. Since a swarm cannot take off until its members have raised the temperature of their thoracic muscles to about 35 °C, a process which takes up to an hour, piping serves as a preparatory signal that precedes departure rather than as a command to depart.

Quorum sensing has a property that consensus lacks: it allows a decision to be implemented before every scout has been persuaded. Because the number of bees present at a site grows fastest at the site with the strongest recruitment, the first site to reach the quorum is, in most cases, the best one; the decision rule, in other words, resembles a race between sites rather than a vote. Hence the swarm can commit while support for inferior sites is still dwindling, without waiting for a unanimity that might never come. Once the flight muscles have been warmed, a further signal, the ‘buzz-run’, in which scouts run through the cluster with their wings buzzing, appears to trigger take-off, and the airborne swarm is guided to the chosen cavity by the few hundred scouts who know its location and who fly rapidly through the cloud of bees in the direction of the site.

The size of the quorum governs a trade-off between speed and accuracy. A high threshold delays commitment until more scouts have independently endorsed a site, which reduces the risk that a site will be chosen on the strength of early, chance-driven support, but it prolongs the period during which the swarm remains exposed; a low threshold has the opposite effect. Experimental evidence is consistent with this account. In trials conducted on a treeless coastal island, where natural cavities were absent, Halvorsen-Teague and Brix (2012) offered swarms a choice between one nest box of 40 litres and four boxes of 15 litres, otherwise identical; the larger box was chosen by 9 of 11 swarms (82%), even though it was outnumbered four to one, and the median decision took 13 hours, spread over two days. In a second series conducted late in the season, under cooler and more changeable weather, the median decision time fell to seven hours, but only 7 of 12 swarms (58%) chose the larger box, a result which the authors tentatively attributed to quorums being reached prematurely. In a control series, in which the 40-litre box was offered against a single 15-litre box, all ten swarms chose the larger box, with a median decision time of nine hours. Moreover, the number of scouts present at the chosen box when piping began was lowest in the late-season series (a mean of 21, against 27 in the first series), a pattern which is consistent with the authors’ interpretation, although it falls short of proving it. Whether swarms actively adjust the quorum to circumstances, as Ishikawa-Moreau’s definition would require, remains uncertain: lower thresholds have been reported in swarms exposed to cold weather (Lindqvist-Obi, 2022), but the evidence comes from only six swarms and has yet to be replicated.

The resemblance between the swarm and the primate brain has been noted repeatedly, and it is closer than most such analogies. In models of perceptual choice, populations of neurons favouring each alternative accumulate evidence over time, inhibit one another and trigger a response when the activity of one population reaches a threshold; in the swarm, groups of scouts accumulate supporters, inhibit one another through stop signals and trigger departure when a quorum is reached. Okafor-Lindqvist (2014) showed that the equations describing the two systems can be made formally identical, and that both reproduce the same speed–accuracy trade-off. The analogy is valuable because it allows hypotheses to travel in both directions: the decay of dancing, for instance, has prompted a search for a comparable ‘leak’ in neural accumulators. Its limit is that formal identity does not entail identity of mechanism. Neurons do not inspect alternatives independently; they receive correlated input, and it is conceivable that the swarm’s reliance on independent assessment has no neural counterpart at all.

The analogy with human groups is both more popular and more problematic. Committees, juries and electorates have been urged to ‘decide like bees’ (Brandvold, 2019), and certain features of the swarm do correspond to well-established findings about group judgement. The accuracy of averaged estimates, often described as the wisdom of crowds, depends, like that of the swarm, on independence: when individuals observe one another’s judgements before forming their own, errors become correlated and the advantage of numbers is largely lost. Conversely, the tendency of cohesive groups to converge prematurely on a shared view, commonly discussed under the heading of groupthink, resembles a swarm in which scouts dance for sites they have never inspected. The swarm, in this sense, offers a model of how a group might be organised to resist groupthink: by separating the gathering of evidence from the expression of support, and by ensuring that support decays unless it is renewed.

The limits of this analogy are, however, considerable. Scouts share a single interest, since all members of a swarm survive or perish together, and the deception, strategic voting and conflicts of interest that characterise many human decisions have no counterpart in the hive. Moreover, the decay of commitment that protects the swarm from early errors depends on a physiological process rather than on deliberate restraint, and there is little evidence that people can be induced to reduce their advocacy at a comparable rate. In a laboratory study in which small groups chose between fictitious apartments, Varga-Thorsen (2021) found that instructing participants to state their preferences only after an independent inspection improved accuracy by 11 percentage points, whereas a rule requiring them to ‘cool’ their advocacy over successive rounds was ignored by most participants. Lessons from the hive, it would seem, are more readily transferred to the design of procedures than to the conduct of individuals.

Robot swarms present the opposite case. Engineers are free to give their agents exactly the rules that the bees follow, and several groups have done so, with encouraging results in controlled settings. In a study by Kowalczyk-Adeyemi (2023), 40 small ground robots, each able to assess only the site at which it stood, selected the better of two charging zones in 87% of trials by means of a quorum rule and a form of cross-inhibition modelled on the stop signal. Performance should not, however, be overstated. Robots share none of the evolutionary history that has tuned the parameters of the bees’ algorithm, and in the same study accuracy fell to 61% when the sensors of a fifth of the robots were deliberately degraded – a sensitivity to faulty individuals that swarms of bees, whose scouts err constantly, do not appear to share. The bees, in other words, offer a tested design, but not one that can be implemented without the parameters that make it work.

Is the honeybee swarm intelligent? The answer depends on the definition adopted. Under the broadest definition, it plainly is, but so is almost any functioning group; under Tobiassen’s, it is, but for reasons that would apply equally to a swarm that chose badly; under Ishikawa-Moreau’s, the case remains open, because it has not been established that swarms adjust their procedure to circumstances. What the evidence reviewed here does establish is more specific and, we believe, more useful: the swarm makes accurate choices among alternatives that no individual compares, and it does so through a combination of independent assessment, recruitment that reflects quality, decay of individual commitment, cross-inhibition and a quorum detected at the site rather than at the cluster.

Our central thesis is that the swarm is better described as a reliable decision mechanism than as an intelligent agent, and that its reliability depends on conditions which are specific and easily lost. Remove independent assessment, and the swarm becomes as vulnerable to cascades as any human crowd; remove the decay of dancing, and early discoveries prevail regardless of quality; lower the quorum too far, and speed is bought at the cost of accuracy. The value of the swarm as a model for human institutions, robotic systems or neural circuits lies less in the label of intelligence than in this inventory of conditions. Analogies that carry the label without the conditions should, in our view, be treated with caution; those that carry the conditions may not need the label at all. Future work would benefit from testing, with larger samples than are currently available, whether swarms do in fact tune their quorum to circumstances, since it is on this question that the stronger claim of intelligence ultimately turns.

questoes.enunciado: Com base no título e no resumo, o tema do artigo é
alternativas: a inteligência coletiva dos insetos sociais e a aplicação de seus mecanismos ao desenho de enxames de robôs e de instituições humanas.
a dança do requebrado e o modo como ela codifica a direção e a distância dos locais de ninho encontrados pelas batedoras.
o modo como enxames de abelhas melíferas escolhem um novo local de ninho e o que esse processo revela, ou não, sobre a “inteligência distribuída”.
o modo como colônias de abelhas melíferas escolhem novas fontes de alimento e o que esse processo revela, ou não, sobre a “inteligência distribuída”.
o consenso a que as batedoras chegam no enxame sobre o novo ninho, tomado como modelo de inteligência para comitês e outros grupos humanos.
questoes.explicacao:
O resumo delimita o objeto e a pergunta: how swarms of the western honeybee choose a new nest site e what, if anything, the process reveals about ‘distributed intelligence’. O título repete os dois eixos (nest-site selection e the limits of ‘distributed intelligence’). Só (c) mantém os dois, inclusive a reserva “ou não” (if anything, limits).

(a) é ampla demais: o texto trata de uma decisão específica de uma espécie, e robôs e instituições são só analogias discutidas na Seção 7. (b) é estreita demais: a dança é um dos quatro mecanismos examinados. (d) troca uma palavra: fontes de alimento no lugar de local de ninho (a dança também serve ao forrageamento, o que torna a troca tentadora). (e) contradiz o texto em dois pontos: a decisão é desencadeada por um quórum no local, não por consenso no enxame (quorum sensing at the candidate site), e os autores criticam justamente o uso do enxame como modelo sem as suas condições.
questoes.dica: Dica: Monte o tema com os elementos do título e do resumo (quem decide, o que decide, que pergunta o artigo faz) e confira cada alternativa elemento por elemento. Quando as alternativas são quase iguais, o erro costuma estar em um só termo (ninho × alimento, quórum × consenso) ou em uma generalização.

questoes.enunciado: No segmento “On the one hand, the swarm must decide quickly […]. On the other hand, it must decide well […]. This double bind is what makes nest-site selection an unusually clean test case for the study of collective decisions” (§2), o segmento destacado refere-se
alternativas: à exigência de que o enxame decida, ao mesmo tempo, depressa e bem.
à escassez do mel carregado pelas operárias, suficiente para três ou quatro dias.
ao risco de escolher uma cavidade pequena, úmida ou exposta demais.
à exposição do aglomerado à chuva, ao frio e aos predadores.
à possibilidade de medir o resultado, registrar o tempo e estimar a informação de cada abelha.
questoes.explicacao:
Double bind (“impasse duplo”, “sinuca”) designa uma situação com duas exigências que se puxam em sentidos opostos. O parágrafo abre anunciando exatamente isso: two requirements that pull in opposite directions, e as desenvolve com On the one hand, the swarm must decide quickly e On the other hand, it must decide well. O segmento resume as duas juntas → (a).

(b) e (d) são as razões da primeira exigência (a pressa), não o impasse inteiro. (c) é a razão da segunda (decidir bem); por estar logo antes do segmento, é a leitura apressada. (e) vem depois e é a consequência: é por causa desse impasse, e de ser mensurável, que o caso serve de teste (Because the outcome can be measured…).
questoes.dica: Dica: Quando “this/these + substantivo” resume algo anterior, use o substantivo como filtro: um double bind exige duas forças opostas; um risk seria só um perigo. Depois descarte as causas de cada lado e a consequência que vem em seguida.

questoes.enunciado:
Na Seção 2 (§4–§6), os autores comparam definições de collective intelligence e swarm intelligence. Associe cada autor à ideia que o texto lhe atribui ou que decorre de sua definição.

  1. Pellegrini-Achebe (2008)
  2. Rasmussen-Okoye (2012)
  3. Dufresne-Kamau (2011)
  4. Tobiassen (2015)
  5. Ishikawa-Moreau (2017)
  • (  )Só chama de inteligente o coletivo cujo modo de decidir muda conforme a situação, por exemplo abrindo mão de precisão quando há pressa.
  • (  )Propõe um critério que, segundo os autores, descreve o que falta aos indivíduos e que seria atendido até por um enxame que escolhesse mal.
  • (  )Exige que o grupo se saia melhor que o seu membro mais competente, exigência que raramente foi posta à prova.
  • (  )Formula a definição mais ampla, que não impõe condição alguma ao modo como o problema é resolvido.
  • (  )Faz o comportamento coerente do grupo decorrer de interações locais entre indivíduos que seguem regras simples, sem acesso a informação global.

Assinale a sequência correta.
questoes.explicacao:
1º: Ishikawa-Moreau (5): intelligent only to the extent that it adjusts its decision procedure to the demands of the situation, for example by trading accuracy for speed when time is short (§6). 2º: Tobiassen (4): sobre o critério dele, os autores dizem It is, however, a negative criterion, which specifies what individuals lack rather than what the group achieves, and it would be satisfied equally well by a swarm that consistently chose poor sites (§5). 3º: Rasmussen-Okoye (2): requiring that the performance of the group exceed that of its best member, a criterion which […] has rarely been tested (§4). 4º: Pellegrini-Achebe (1): it sets no condition on how the problem is solved (§4). 5º: Dufresne-Kamau (3): coherent group-level behaviour arises from local interactions among individuals that follow simple rules and have no access to global information (§5).

Armadilhas: Dufresne-Kamau e Tobiassen estão no mesmo parágrafo e ambos falam do que os indivíduos não têm (informação global × representação do problema), daí a troca 3/4 em e. Pellegrini-Achebe e Rasmussen-Okoye estão ambos no §4 e tratam do desempenho (troca 1/2 em e).

Nas alternativas erradas: (a) erra os itens 1, 2, 3, 4 e 5; (b) erra os itens 2 e 3; (c) erra os itens 1, 3, 4 e 5; (d) erra os itens 1 e 5.
questoes.dica: Dica: Em associação de autores, ache o verbo ou a exigência central de cada definição (solve problems none could solve alone, exceed its best member, local interactions, no individual holds a representation, adjusts its procedure) e compare com as paráfrases. Autores do mesmo parágrafo costumam ser trocados entre si: resolva ao menos três itens antes de marcar.

questoes.enunciado: A função do segmento destacado em “Alongside these definitions, a looser usage has spread […], in which ‘swarm intelligence’ is applied to almost any coordinated behaviour of many agents, such as the trail networks of ants, the synchronised flashing of fireflies and the price movements of financial markets” (§7) é
alternativas: enumerar os sistemas cujos mecanismos são examinados nas seções seguintes do artigo.
exemplificar comportamentos coordenados muito distintos aos quais o uso frouxo do termo se aplica.
ilustrar fenômenos que, segundo os autores, compartilham o mecanismo de decisão do enxame de abelhas.
apresentar os sistemas de engenharia que compõem a amostra de 164 artigos de Vasquez-Lindholm (2020).
restringir o termo aos casos que satisfazem as definições de Dufresne-Kamau e de Tobiassen.
questoes.explicacao:
Such as (“como, por exemplo”) introduz exemplos de almost any coordinated behaviour of many agents. A escolha de casos díspares (trilhas de formigas, vaga-lumes, mercados financeiros) serve para mostrar a amplitude do uso frouxo, que os autores criticam logo depois (The cost of this extension is not merely terminological) → (b).

(a) as seções seguintes tratam só das abelhas; formigas, vaga-lumes e mercados não são examinados. (c) inverte o texto: o problema é aplicar o rótulo a phenomena that share no mechanism. (d) os 164 artigos de Vasquez-Lindholm tratam de engineered systems; os exemplos não são essa amostra, e um deles nem é engenharia; é a leitura apressada de quem junta as duas frases do parágrafo. (e) a restrição do termo vem no fim do parágrafo (the term is accordingly used in the restricted sense), e os exemplos ilustram justamente o uso que os autores não adotam.
questoes.dica: Dica: Para a função de um segmento, pergunte o que ele faz com a frase em que está: such as, for instance, e.g. introduzem exemplos de um termo geral que vem antes (aqui, coordinated behaviour). Depois veja com que intenção o autor escolheu esses exemplos, olhando a frase seguinte.

questoes.enunciado: Os segmentos destacados em “[…] a few dozen of the colony’s older foragers begin to inspect potential cavities, and once the cluster has formed, their number rises to between 300 and 500 […]” (§8), “Those preferences are not arbitrary” (§9) e “Volume, for instance, is thought to be estimated from the distance walked inside the cavity, which would explain why scouts spend much of their first visit on foot rather than on the wing” (§9) referem-se, respectivamente, a
alternativas: the colony’s older foragers – potential cavities – a ideia de que o volume é estimado pela distância percorrida dentro da cavidade.

the colony’s older foragers – características que predominavam nas cavidades ocupadas no levantamento de Nwachukwu-Sorensen – a ideia de que o volume é estimado pela distância percorrida dentro da cavidade.
a preferência das populações temperadas do hemisfério norte por entradas voltadas para o sul – potential cavities – the distance walked inside the cavity.
a preferência das populações temperadas do hemisfério norte por entradas voltadas para o sul – potential cavities – a ideia de que o volume é estimado pela distância percorrida dentro da cavidade.
the colony’s older foragers – características que predominavam nas cavidades ocupadas no levantamento de Nwachukwu-Sorensen – the distance walked inside the cavity.
questoes.explicacao:
their: o número que sobe para 300 a 500 é o das operárias que fazem a inspeção, isto é, the colony’s older foragers, que então são chamadas de scouts. potential cavities é o substantivo plural mais próximo, mas o próprio §8 diz que só between 10 and 30 potential sites are discovered, e a frase completa o raciocínio com roughly three to five per cent of the swarm, uma fração de abelhas.

Those preferences: resume o conjunto de características encontradas na maioria das cavidades ocupadas (volume de 30 a 60 litros, entrada pequena, perto do piso, a três metros do solo e, nas populações temperadas, voltada para o sul). A frase seguinte justifica várias delas (volume, entrada pequena, entrada alta), o que mostra que o referente não é só a orientação para o sul, a mais próxima.

which: depois de vírgula, retoma a oração inteira: é o fato de o volume ser estimado pela distância percorrida que explicaria por que as batedoras passam a primeira visita andando. A distância em si (the distance walked) não explica nada; o que explica é o método de medição.

Nas alternativas erradas: (a) erra o item 2; (c) erra os itens 1, 2 e 3; (d) erra os itens 1 e 2; (e) erra o item 3.
questoes.dica: Dica: Para cada pronome, teste o candidato no lugar dele (“o número de cavidades sobe para 300 a 500?”) e confira com os dados vizinhos. Em those/these + substantivo, veja quantas ideias a frase seguinte comenta. Em , which, pergunte se o que vem depois (aqui, “explicaria por que…”) pode ser feito por um substantivo ou só por uma oração inteira.

questoes.enunciado:
Indique se os segmentos a seguir estão em acordo (A) ou desacordo (D) com o que apresentam os parágrafos 8 a 10.

  • (  )Antes mesmo de o enxame deixar o ninho de origem, algumas dezenas de operárias mais velhas já começam a examinar possíveis cavidades.
  • (  )As batedoras representam cerca de 3% a 5% do enxame, e as demais abelhas se revezam com elas na busca para poupar energia.
  • (  )No levantamento de Nwachukwu-Sorensen (2013), a maior parte das cavidades ocupadas tinha a entrada perto do teto e a pelo menos três metros do solo.
  • (  )Segundo Feldmann-Ortiz (2016), as raras batedoras que visitaram mais de um local não se mostraram mais propensas que as outras a apoiar o melhor deles.

Assinale a sequência correta.
alternativas: D – A – A – D
A – A – A – A
A – A – A – D
A – D – D – A
D – D – D – A
questoes.explicacao:
1 (A): paráfrase de In the days preceding departure, a few dozen of the colony’s older foragers begin to inspect potential cavities (§8).

2 (D): a porcentagem está certa, mas as demais não participam: The remaining bees take no part in the search: they hang quietly in the cluster, conserving energy (§8). Poupar energia é o que fazem ficando paradas, não revezando.

3 (D): a altura em relação ao solo está certa, mas a posição da entrada é a oposta: located near the floor of the cavity (§9).

4 (A): paráfrase de fewer than 5% of scouts visited more than one candidate site […], and those that did were no more likely than the others to support the better of the two (§10).

Cada alternativa errada difere da certa em um único item, por isso é preciso conferir os quatro.

Nas alternativas erradas: (a) erra os itens 1, 2, 3 e 4; (b) erra os itens 2 e 3; (c) erra os itens 2, 3 e 4; (e) erra o item 1.
questoes.dica: Dica: Nos itens de A/D, divida cada afirmação em partes (quem, quantos, onde, quando) e confira uma por uma. Um item com um número certo pode esconder um detalhe trocado na outra metade (perto do piso × do teto; ficam paradas × se revezam).

questoes.enunciado: O segmento destacado em “The danger is reduced by a feature that has proved central to every subsequent model of the process: the gradual decline in the number of waggle runs performed by each returning scout” (§13) pode ser traduzido, no contexto em que é empregado, por
alternativas: o declínio gradual no número de corridas de requebrado executadas por cada batedora que retorna.
o número de declínios graduais nas corridas de requebrado executadas por cada batedora que retorna.
o declínio gradual das batedoras que retornam depois de executar as corridas de requebrado.
o declínio gradual no número de batedoras que retornam e executam corridas de requebrado.
o número gradualmente menor de corridas de requebrado que cada batedora executa antes de retornar.
questoes.explicacao:
O núcleo é decline (declínio), qualificado por gradual; in the number of waggle runs diz em que há declínio (no número de corridas de requebrado); o particípio pós-nominal performed by each returning scout qualifica waggle runs (corridas executadas por cada batedora); e returning, antes de scout, funciona como adjetivo (“que retorna”).

(b) troca o núcleo para number. (c) faz das batedoras o que declina e transforma performed em ação anterior ao retorno. (d) desloca number para as batedoras: o que diminui são as corridas de cada uma, não quantas batedoras voltam; o parágrafo confirma (a scout dances somewhat less than on the previous one). (e) muda o núcleo e o momento: as danças são feitas na volta, no enxame, não antes de retornar.
questoes.dica: Dica: Ache o núcleo (geralmente o substantivo antes da primeira preposição: decline) e pendure nele, em ordem, cada complemento: in the number of X (em quê), X performed by Y (particípio que qualifica o substantivo imediatamente anterior). Um -ing antes do substantivo (returning scout) é adjetivo: “batedora que retorna”.

questoes.enunciado:
Considere os seguintes segmentos do texto:

I - “The decline thus functions as a kind of forgetting, which prevents the swarm from becoming locked into its first impressions” (§13)II - “the number of bees committed to each site grows at a rate that reflects its quality” (§12)III - “the stop signal is the closest thing the hive has to heckling a rival speaker” (§14)IV - “a high-pitched vibration which stimulates the quiescent bees to warm their flight muscles” (§16)

É(São) exemplo(s) de linguagem metafórica, ou seja, figurada, para se referir ao processo de decisão do enxame
alternativas: apenas I e III.
apenas I, II e III.
apenas III e IV.
apenas I e IV.
apenas II e IV.
questoes.explicacao:
I (figurado): o declínio das danças é um processo fisiológico; chamá-lo de forgetting (esquecer) e falar em first impressions (primeiras impressões) atribui ao enxame faculdades mentais que ele não tem.

II (literal): descreve um fato mensurável: o número de abelhas comprometidas com cada local cresce a uma taxa que reflete sua qualidade. Committed aqui significa apenas “que passaram a apoiar/visitar aquele local”.

III (figurado): heckling a rival speaker (vaiar/interromper um orador rival) transfere para a colmeia a imagem de um debate humano; a abelha apenas vibra e bate a cabeça na dançarina.

IV (literal): descreve o sinal de piping como vibração aguda que leva as abelhas a aquecer os músculos de voo, sem comparação nem transferência de sentido.

Logo, apenas I e III (a). (b) inclui II, que é literal; (c) exclui I e inclui IV; (d) troca III por IV; (e) reúne justamente os dois segmentos literais.
questoes.dica: Dica: Pergunte se o segmento descreve o que as abelhas fazem fisicamente (literal) ou se empresta vocabulário de outro domínio, como mente, política ou debate humano, para falar delas (figurado). Termos técnicos já consagrados, ainda que vívidos, contam como literais no contexto.

questoes.enunciado:
Considere os segmentos sublinhados a seguir.

I - “The danger is reduced by a feature that has proved central to every subsequent model of the process” (§13)II - “In a study in which two nest boxes of equal quality were offered, Andrade-Kowalczyk (2019) found […]” (§14)III - “it is from this foraging signal that the one used during nest-site selection has probably been derived” (§14)IV - “small random differences between the two groups of supporters are amplified” (§15)

Os segmentos sublinhados estão, respectivamente, nos seguintes tempos e vozes verbais:
alternativas: presente perfeito, voz ativa – passado simples, voz ativa – presente perfeito, voz passiva – presente simples, voz ativa.
presente perfeito, voz passiva – passado simples, voz passiva – presente perfeito, voz passiva – presente simples, voz ativa.
presente perfeito, voz passiva – passado simples, voz ativa – passado perfeito, voz passiva – presente simples, voz passiva.
presente perfeito, voz ativa – passado simples, voz passiva – presente perfeito, voz passiva – presente simples, voz passiva.
presente perfeito, voz passiva – passado simples, voz passiva – passado perfeito, voz passiva – presente simples, voz passiva.
questoes.explicacao:
I: has proved = has + particípio de prove, sem o verbo be: presente perfeito, voz ativa (o sujeito a feature “mostrou-se” central). O particípio sozinho não torna a forma passiva.

II: were offered = were + particípio: passado simples, voz passiva (as caixas foram oferecidas pelos pesquisadores).

III: has probably been derived = has been + particípio, com o advérbio intercalado: presente perfeito, voz passiva. Não é passado perfeito, que exigiria had been.

IV: are amplified = are + particípio: presente simples, voz passiva.

Erros das demais: (a) põe II e IV na ativa; (b) põe I na passiva e IV na ativa; (c) põe I na passiva, II na ativa e confunde III com passado perfeito; (e) põe I na passiva e confunde III com passado perfeito.
questoes.dica: Dica: Para a voz passiva, procure be (em qualquer forma: is, are, was, were, been, being) seguido de particípio. Has/have + particípio sem been é presente perfeito ativo. O tempo é dado pelo auxiliar: has/have = presente perfeito; had = passado perfeito.

questoes.enunciado: Em “[…] the first site to reach the quorum is, in most cases, the best one; the decision rule, in other words, resembles a race between sites rather than a vote. Hence the swarm can commit while support for inferior sites is still dwindling […]” (§17), o conector sublinhado pode ser substituído, sem alteração de sentido, por
alternativas: Henceforth
Nonetheless
Meanwhile
Therefore
Likewise
questoes.explicacao:
Hence = “daí, por isso, portanto”: introduz uma conclusão/consequência. Como a decisão funciona como uma corrida (o primeiro local a atingir o quórum vence), o enxame pode se comprometer sem esperar que o apoio aos locais piores se extinga. Therefore mantém essa relação.

(a) Henceforth (“de agora em diante”) é a armadilha da forma parecida: indica tempo, não consequência. (b) Nonetheless (“ainda assim”) indicaria concessão/contraste, como se a frase contrariasse a anterior. (c) Meanwhile (“enquanto isso”) indica simultaneidade; a palavra while, dentro da frase, torna a opção tentadora. (e) Likewise (“da mesma forma”) indica comparação/adição.
questoes.dica: Dica: Para testar uma substituição, reescreva a frase com cada alternativa e veja se a relação continua a mesma (causa, consequência, concessão, tempo, adição). Desconfie de palavras com a mesma raiz e sentido diferente (hence × henceforth) e de alternativas que ecoam uma palavra da própria frase.

questoes.enunciado:
Indique se os segmentos a seguir estão em acordo (A) ou desacordo (D) com o que apresenta o §18 sobre os experimentos de escolha de ninho.

  • (  )Na primeira série, a caixa de 40 litros foi escolhida por 9 dos 11 enxames, e a decisão mediana levou sete horas, ao longo de dois dias.
  • (  )Na série realizada mais tarde na estação, os enxames decidiram quase duas vezes mais depressa que na primeira, mas pouco mais da metade deles ficou com a caixa maior.
  • (  )O número menor de batedoras presentes na caixa escolhida quando o piping começou, registrado na série tardia, comprova que nela os quóruns foram atingidos cedo demais.
  • (  )Ainda não se sabe se os enxames regulam ativamente o quórum conforme as condições, pois a indicação de limiares menores sob frio vem de poucos enxames e não foi reproduzida.

Assinale a sequência correta.
alternativas: A – A – A – A
A – D – A – D
D – A – A – D
D – D – D – A
D – A – D – A
questoes.explicacao:
1 (D): a proporção está certa (the larger box was chosen by 9 of 11 swarms (82%)), mas o tempo é o de outra série: na primeira, the median decision took 13 hours, spread over two days; as sete horas são da série tardia (the median decision time fell to seven hours, §18).

2 (A): paráfrase de the median decision time fell to seven hours, but only 7 of 12 swarms (58%) chose the larger box (§18): 7 horas contra 13 é quase a metade do tempo, e 58% é pouco mais da metade.

3 (D): o dado existe (lowest in the late-season series (a mean of 21, against 27 in the first series)), mas o texto não diz que ele comprova a hipótese: a pattern which is consistent with the authors’ interpretation, although it falls short of proving it; e os próprios autores a apresentaram tentatively (§18).

4 (A): paráfrase de Whether swarms actively adjust the quorum to circumstances […] remains uncertain: lower thresholds have been reported in swarms exposed to cold weather (Lindqvist-Obi, 2022), but the evidence comes from only six swarms and has yet to be replicated (§18).

Nas alternativas erradas: (a) erra os itens 1 e 3; (b) erra os itens 1, 2, 3 e 4; (c) erra os itens 3 e 4; (d) erra o item 2.
questoes.dica: Dica: Quando um parágrafo relata várias séries ou condições de um experimento, anote qual número pertence a cada uma antes de julgar os itens: um item pode juntar um dado certo de uma série com outro de outra. Compare também o verbo do item (comprova, confirma) com o grau de certeza do texto (é compatível com, sugere, tentativamente).

questoes.enunciado:
Considere as seguintes afirmações sobre a Seção 7, Lessons beyond the hive (§19–§22).

I - Embora as equações que descrevem o enxame e as populações de neurônios possam ser tornadas formalmente idênticas, os autores advertem que isso não basta para concluir que os mecanismos sejam os mesmos.II - Para os autores, o enxame sugere como um grupo humano poderia resistir ao pensamento de grupo: separando a coleta de evidências da manifestação de apoio e fazendo o apoio esmorecer se não for renovado.III - No estudo de Varga-Thorsen (2021), a regra que pedia aos participantes que moderassem gradualmente sua defesa ao longo das rodadas elevou a acurácia em 11 pontos percentuais.IV - Quando os sensores de um quinto dos robôs foram propositalmente prejudicados, a taxa de acerto caiu de 87% para 61%, fragilidade que os enxames de abelhas não parecem compartilhar.

Estão em acordo com o texto
alternativas: apenas II e IV.
apenas I e III.
apenas III.
apenas I, II e III.
apenas I, II e IV.
questoes.explicacao:
I (acordo): Okafor-Lindqvist (2014) showed that the equations describing the two systems can be made formally identical; e Its limit is that formal identity does not entail identity of mechanism (§19).

II (acordo): offers a model of how a group might be organised to resist groupthink: by separating the gathering of evidence from the expression of support, and by ensuring that support decays unless it is renewed (§20).

III (desacordo): os 11 pontos vieram de outra regra, a de declarar preferências só depois de uma inspeção independente; a regra de “esfriar” a defesa was ignored by most participants (§21).

IV (acordo): selected the better of two charging zones in 87% of trials e accuracy fell to 61% when the sensors of a fifth of the robots were deliberately degraded – a sensitivity to faulty individuals that swarms of bees […] do not appear to share (§22).

Nas alternativas erradas: (a) deixa de fora I, que está correta; (b) inclui III, que é falsa, e deixa de fora II e IV, que estão corretas; (c) inclui III, que é falsa, e deixa de fora I, II e IV, que estão corretas; (d) inclui III, que é falsa, e deixa de fora IV, que está correta.
questoes.dica: Dica: Julgue cada afirmação isoladamente antes de olhar as alternativas. Quando um estudo testa duas condições, confira a que condição cada resultado pertence: o número certo atribuído à condição errada é uma das trocas mais comuns.

questoes.enunciado: Assinale a alternativa cujo segmento sublinhado expressa uma possibilidade (e não certeza, necessidade nem recomendação).
alternativas: “Since a swarm <u>cannot</u> take off until its members have raised the temperature of their thoracic muscles to about 35 °C […]” (§16).
“On the one hand, the swarm <u>must</u> decide quickly […]” (§2).
“[…] <u>it is conceivable that</u> the swarm’s reliance on independent assessment has no neural counterpart at all” (§19).
“Performance <u>should not</u>, however, be overstated” (§22).
“Under the broadest definition, it <u>plainly</u> is […]” (§23).
questoes.explicacao:
It is conceivable that (“é concebível que, é possível que”) apresenta a falta de equivalente neural como hipótese que não pode ser descartada, sem afirmá-la: é possibilidade.

(a) é a armadilha: cannot é forma de can, mas aqui expressa uma impossibilidade física apresentada como certa (o enxame não decola sem aquecer os músculos). (b) must expressa necessidade imposta pela situação (o mel dura três ou quatro dias). (d) should not é recomendação (“não se deve superestimar”). (e) plainly (“claramente, evidentemente”) marca certeza.
questoes.dica: Dica: Classifique cada modalizador antes de comparar: certeza (plainly, cannot no sentido de impossível), necessidade (must, have to), recomendação (should, ought to), possibilidade (it is conceivable that, perhaps, may). Uma forma negativa de “poder” (cannot) costuma indicar impossibilidade com certeza, não possibilidade.

questoes.enunciado: Na Seção 7 (§19–§22), os autores apontam limites das analogias entre o enxame e outros sistemas. Qual elemento NÃO é apresentado como um desses limites?
alternativas: Os neurônios recebem informação correlacionada e não avaliam as alternativas de forma independente.
As batedoras erram com frequência em suas avaliações, o que torna o enxame um modelo pouco seguro para engenheiros.
Os grupos humanos convivem com engano, voto estratégico e conflitos de interesse, que não existem entre as batedoras.
Os robôs não têm a história evolutiva que ajustou os parâmetros do algoritmo seguido pelas abelhas.
Nas abelhas, o enfraquecimento do compromisso decorre de um processo fisiológico, e não de autocontenção deliberada.
questoes.explicacao:
(a) é o limite da analogia neural: Neurons do not inspect alternatives independently; they receive correlated input (§19). (c) e (e) são os limites da analogia humana: the deception, strategic voting and conflicts of interest […] have no counterpart in the hive e depends on a physiological process rather than on deliberate restraint (§21). (d) é o limite da analogia com robôs: Robots share none of the evolutionary history that has tuned the parameters of the bees’ algorithm (§22).

(b) é o intruso. O texto menciona que as batedoras erram (whose scouts err constantly, §22), mas para mostrar o oposto: mesmo com indivíduos falhos, o enxame de abelhas não perde a confiabilidade, ao contrário dos robôs. Quem reconhece a expressão sem ler a frase inteira marca a alternativa errada.
questoes.dica: Dica: Em questões de NÃO, confira cada alternativa contra a frase exata do texto. O intruso costuma usar uma informação que está lá (aqui, “as batedoras erram”), mas com a função invertida: o que o texto apresenta como vantagem aparece como limite.

questoes.enunciado: Assinale a alternativa que apresenta uma informação FALSA de acordo com o texto.
alternativas: Estima-se que o mel levado pelas operárias no estômago baste para manter o aglomerado por, no máximo, três ou quatro dias (§2).
Na corrida do requebrado, é o tempo de vibração, e não a inclinação, que informa a que distância fica a cavidade, numa proporção aproximada de um segundo por quilômetro (§11).
As batedoras começam a emitir o piping quando percebem que o número de companheiras dançando pelo mesmo local no aglomerado chegou a algo entre 20 e 30 abelhas (§16).
Num experimento com apartamentos fictícios, exigir que os participantes só declarassem preferência depois de uma inspeção independente aumentou a acurácia em 11 pontos percentuais (§21).
Robôs que só avaliavam o local onde estavam escolheram a melhor zona de recarga em 87% dos ensaios, mas o desempenho caiu quando parte dos sensores foi degradada (§22).
questoes.explicacao:
(c) é a falsa: o quórum é percebido no próprio local, não no aglomerado. Scouts visiting a cavity appear to monitor the number of other scouts present there, and once that number reaches a threshold – estimated at between 20 and 30 bees; e, antes, No consensus is ever registered at the cluster (§16).

As demais são verdadeiras: (a) sustain the cluster for no more than three or four days (§2); (b) Its duration, by contrast, encodes distance, at a rate of roughly one second of waggling for each kilometre, enquanto o ângulo indica a direção (§11); (d) instructing participants to state their preferences only after an independent inspection improved accuracy by 11 percentage points (§21); (e) selected the better of two charging zones in 87% of trials e accuracy fell to 61% when the sensors of a fifth of the robots were deliberately degraded (§22).
questoes.dica: Dica: Em “assinale a FALSA”, confira cada afirmação no parágrafo indicado, palavra por palavra: o erro costuma estar num detalhe (onde, quem, quanto, direção × distância), enquanto o resto da frase repete fielmente o texto.

questoes.enunciado: Qual alternativa sintetiza a conclusão dos autores (§23–§24)?
alternativas: O enxame é inteligente segundo todas as definições examinadas, já que escolhe bem entre alternativas que nenhuma abelha compara.
Como o rótulo de inteligência é impreciso, as analogias entre o enxame e outros sistemas devem ser abandonadas.
O enxame é antes um mecanismo de decisão confiável que um agente inteligente, e seu valor como modelo está nas condições frágeis de que depende.
A confiabilidade do enxame resulta do consenso alcançado entre as dançarinas antes da partida, condição que outros sistemas raramente reproduzem.
Já se demonstrou que os enxames ajustam o quórum às circunstâncias, o que sustenta a afirmação mais forte de que são inteligentes.
questoes.explicacao:
(c) reúne a tese (the swarm is better described as a reliable decision mechanism than as an intelligent agent, and that its reliability depends on conditions which are specific and easily lost) e a consequência para as analogias (The value of the swarm as a model […] lies less in the label of intelligence than in this inventory of conditions) (§24).

(a) contradiz o §23: pela definição de Ishikawa-Moreau, the case remains open. (b) generaliza demais: só as analogias that carry the label without the conditions pedem cautela; as que levam as condições may not need the label at all. (d) troca o mecanismo: o quórum é detectado at the site rather than at the cluster, sem consenso. (e) apresenta como demonstrado o que os autores pedem que seja testado (Future work would benefit from testing […] whether swarms do in fact tune their quorum).
questoes.dica: Dica: Na conclusão, confira cada alternativa contra uma frase específica dos últimos parágrafos. Os distratores mais fortes generalizam uma ressalva (cautela com algumas analogias → abandonar todas) ou transformam uma pergunta em aberto em resultado demonstrado.
